To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) bumblebees are not lifetime specialists, 2) most foragers are specialists over short time periods, 3) larger bees make more foraging bouts, 4) antennal morphology is associated with foraging bout number, but not with specialization.

(i) bumblebee colonies show a high degree of specialization over short timescales, (ii) the majority of foragers in a colony do not specialize on a given reward over their lifetime, (iii) larger foragers and foragers with more antennal sensilla make more foraging bouts, but are not more likely to be specialists, and (iv) there is no evidence that foragers that are specialists are more efficient at foraging.
bumblebees show short- and long-term specialization in pollen and nectar collection and that this specialization does not relate to foraging success.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how foraging patterns are generated by individuals in social insect colonies and how they contribute to colony-level performance.
how foraging specialization emerges and is maintained over time.
the evolution of specialization in a social context.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

short-term reward specialization by bumblebee workers is not associated with any particular morphological trait, but that the proportion of foragers specializing daily on a given resource type varies between species and colonies, and that it is not associated with foraging success.
short term specialization is common in bumblebees and is not associated with better performance, and that the causes of specialization are not well understood.
bumblebees do not specialize in pollen and nectar collection over timescales of a day or a lifetime, but do so over timescales of minutes or hours.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the foraging patterns of bumblebees are complex, and that the factors that influence these patterns are not necessarily those that influence lifetime task specialization.

bumblebees are not highly task specialist, and that short-term patterns of specialization may be more a result of individual differences in foraging success than of a mechanism for improving colony foraging efficiency.
short-term reward specialization in bumblebees is a common, but not necessarily adaptive, phenomenon.
The main takeaway from our work is that
foraging behaviour in eusocial bees is not necessarily a simple reflection of worker size, but rather is a complex function of the environment and the colony.

forager specialization is common over timescales shorter and longer than lifetime, and that foragers with more olfactory sensilla are more efficient foragers, regardless of whether they specialize on pollen or nectar.
bumblebee foragers are highly flexible and can rapidly adjust their foraging behaviour to match colony needs.
